title: Agency & Fiduciary Duties
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.
note: Enlarged bank (20 items) because Laws of Agency & Fiduciary Duties is ~17% of the state exam.

questions.stem: When a salesperson obtains a listing, the agency relationship legally exists between the seller and:
options: The salesperson personally
The salesperson's employing broker
The multiple listing service
Both the salesperson and the broker as co-agents
rationales: The salesperson acts for the broker; the listing does not belong to the salesperson.
Correct. The broker is the agent of the client, and the salesperson is the broker's associate licensee — which is why dual agency arises at the brokerage level.
The MLS is a private listing database, not a party to the agency.
There is one agent — the broker — not two co-agents.

questions.stem: In OLD CAR, which duty requires an agent to protect the principal's motivation and financial condition from the other side?
options: Obedience
Disclosure
Confidentiality
Accounting
rationales: Obedience concerns following lawful instructions.
Disclosure requires telling the *principal* material information — the opposite direction.
Correct. Confidentiality protects the principal's confidential information, including motivation and the lowest price they would accept, and it survives termination of the agency.
Accounting concerns funds and property entrusted to the agent.

questions.stem: A seller instructs the listing agent not to present offers from buyers with young children. The agent should:
options: Comply, because obedience is a fiduciary duty
Comply, but document the instruction in the file
Refuse, because the instruction is unlawful discrimination
Present the offers but recommend the seller reject them
rationales: Obedience extends only to lawful instructions.
Documenting an unlawful instruction does not make following it lawful.
Correct. Familial status is a protected class; the agent must refuse the instruction and should advise the seller of the law, withdrawing if the seller persists.
Steering the seller toward rejecting protected-class buyers is the same violation in another form.

questions.stem: A listing agent learns the buyer is willing to pay $30,000 more than the offer submitted. The agent must:
options: Keep it confidential to protect the transaction
Disclose it to the seller under the duty of disclosure
Disclose it only if the seller specifically asks
Disclose it to the buyer's agent first
rationales: The agent owes confidentiality to the *seller*, not the buyer; protecting the deal is not a recognized duty.
Correct. The duty of disclosure requires telling the principal all material information affecting their interests, including a buyer's greater willingness to pay.
The duty is affirmative and does not depend on the client asking.
The information belongs to the seller's side of the analysis; disclosing it to the buyer's agent serves no duty.

questions.stem: A brokerage lists a home; a different salesperson at the SAME brokerage represents the buyer. This situation is:
options: Not dual agency, because different salespersons are involved
Dual agency at the brokerage level, requiring informed written consent from both parties
Subagency
Prohibited in California under all circumstances
rationales: Assigning different salespersons manages the conflict but does not eliminate brokerage-level dual agency.
Correct. Because the broker is the agent of both clients, dual agency exists and requires informed written consent from buyer and seller.
Subagency involves an agent of the agent, typically a cooperating broker acting for the seller.
Dual agency is lawful in California with informed written consent.

questions.stem: A properly consented dual agent knows the sellers are financially distressed and that the roof leaks. The dual agent may disclose to the buyer:
options: Both the distress and the leak
The leak only
The distress only
Neither, without written permission
rationales: Financial distress is confidential motivation that a dual agent may not reveal without permission.
Correct. Property condition is never confidential — known material defects must be disclosed — while the sellers' financial motivation must be protected.
This reverses the rule: motivation is protected and condition is disclosed.
Material defects must be disclosed regardless of permission; silence would be concealment.

questions.stem: An agent lists a property and, without disclosing his ownership interest, arranges for an LLC he partly owns to purchase it below market. The agent's gain on resale is recoverable by the seller as a:
options: Referral fee
Secret profit
Liquidated damage
Commission override
rationales: A referral fee is disclosed compensation for referring business.
Correct. An undisclosed benefit derived from the agency is a secret profit, recoverable by the principal and grounds for license discipline.
Liquidated damages are contractual pre-agreed damages for breach.
A commission override is a share of commission paid within a brokerage structure.

questions.stem: Which statement is PUFFING rather than a representation of fact?
options: 'This home is zoned for commercial use.'
'The roof was replaced in 2021.'
'This is the most charming street in Claremont.'
'The lot is 8,400 square feet.'
rationales: Zoning is verifiable fact; misstating it is misrepresentation.
Roof age is a verifiable fact.
Correct. An exaggerated subjective opinion no reasonable buyer would rely on as fact is puffing.
Lot size is a verifiable fact and a frequent source of misrepresentation claims.

questions.stem: An agent innocently tells a buyer the home has permitted square footage of 2,400 based on an outdated flyer. The permitted area is 1,950. The agent is:
options: Not liable, because the statement was innocent
Potentially liable, because even innocent misrepresentation of a material fact can support rescission or damages
Liable only if the buyer can prove intent to deceive
Protected because square footage is always considered puffing
rationales: Lack of intent limits some remedies but does not eliminate liability.
Correct. Innocent, negligent, and intentional misrepresentations can all create liability; a competent agent verifies square footage rather than repeating a flyer.
Intent is required for fraud, not for all misrepresentation remedies.
Square footage is a verifiable fact, never puffing.

questions.stem: Agency created when a principal's own conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe someone represents them is called:
options: Implied agency
Ostensible agency
Ratification
Express agency
rationales: Implied agency arises from the conduct of the parties to the relationship itself.
Correct. Ostensible (apparent) agency arises from the principal's conduct causing a third party's reasonable belief.
Ratification is after-the-fact approval of an unauthorized act.
Express agency arises from a written or spoken agreement.

questions.stem: An unauthorized person negotiates a lease for an owner. Learning all the facts, the owner accepts the rent and honors the lease. The agency was created by:
options: Estoppel
Ratification
Necessity
Subagency
rationales: Estoppel concerns preventing a party from denying a state of affairs they created; the facts describe after-the-fact acceptance.
Correct. Accepting the benefits of an unauthorized act with knowledge of the facts ratifies it, binding the principal.
Necessity is a doctrine for easements, not agency creation here.
Subagency describes an agent of an agent.

questions.stem: A real estate broker hired to find a buyer for one specific property is acting as a:
options: General agent
Universal agent
Special agent
Subagent
rationales: A general agent has ongoing authority over a range of matters, like a property manager.
A universal agent may act in all matters, typically under a broad power of attorney.
Correct. A broker engaged for one transaction with limited authority is a special agent — the usual real estate role.
A subagent is an agent of the agent.

questions.stem: While showing a 1948 home, an agent sees a large brown ceiling stain under an upstairs bathroom, freshly painted over. The seller's TDS discloses no leaks. The agent must:
options: Say nothing, since the TDS is the seller's disclosure
Disclose the observation in writing to the buyer and recommend further inspection
Diagnose the cause and estimate repair cost for the buyer
Report the seller to the DRE before proceeding
rationales: The agent's own visual inspection duty is independent of the seller's TDS.
Correct. The duty of reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection of accessible areas requires disclosing observed red flags and referring the buyer to a qualified inspector.
Agents are not inspectors and must not diagnose causes or estimate repair costs.
The immediate obligation is disclosure to the buyer, not a regulatory complaint.

questions.stem: A seller contributes to the compensation of the buyer's brokerage. This payment:
options: Makes the buyer's broker an agent of the seller
Creates dual agency automatically
Does not change who the buyer's broker represents
Requires the buyer's broker to disclose the buyer's maximum price
rationales: Compensation does not create agency; representation flows from the agency agreement.
No dual agency arises merely because the seller contributed to compensation.
Correct. Who pays and who is represented are separate questions — the buyer's broker continues to owe full fiduciary duties to the buyer.
Disclosing the buyer's maximum price would breach confidentiality owed to the buyer.

questions.stem: To a third party (customer) in the transaction, a licensee owes:
options: Loyalty and confidentiality
Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts
The same fiduciary duties owed to a principal
No duties whatsoever
rationales: Loyalty and confidentiality run to the principal only.
Correct. Third parties are owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts, but not fiduciary duties.
Fiduciary duties are reserved for the principal.
Licensees always owe third parties honesty and material-fact disclosure.

questions.stem: California's agency disclosure process for residential 1–4 unit sales is best summarized as:
options: Advertise, negotiate, close
Disclose, elect, confirm
Notify, record, verify
Present, accept, ratify
rationales: These are transaction activities, not the statutory agency disclosure steps.
Correct. The licensee delivers the agency disclosure form, elects in writing which party is represented, and confirms the relationships in writing with the purchase contract.
Recording concerns documents affecting title, not agency disclosure.
These describe contract formation, not agency disclosure.

questions.stem: An exclusive listing agreement that contains NO definite termination date is:
options: Valid, because listings run until the property sells
Grounds for disciplinary action against the licensee
Automatically converted to an open listing
Valid if the seller initials the omission
rationales: Open-ended exclusive listings are exactly what the rule prohibits.
Correct. An exclusive listing must specify a definite termination date; omitting one is grounds for discipline.
No automatic conversion occurs.
The seller cannot waive the requirement by initialing.

questions.stem: After a listing expires unsold, the former listing agent may:
options: Freely tell prospective buyers the lowest price the seller would have accepted
Not disclose the seller's confidential information, because confidentiality survives termination
Disclose confidential information after six months
Disclose it only to other licensees
rationales: Termination of the agency does not release the agent to reveal what was learned in confidence.
Correct. The duty of confidentiality survives the end of the agency relationship.
No waiting period converts confidential information into public information.
The identity of the recipient does not matter; the information remains protected.

questions.stem: At an open house, a listing agent counsels a visiting unrepresented buyer on offer strategy, reveals the seller must close by September, and suggests offering below asking. The agent has MOST likely:
options: Provided good customer service consistent with fair dealing
Breached confidentiality and loyalty, and risked creating an undisclosed dual agency
Created a valid buyer representation agreement
Committed puffing
rationales: Fair dealing requires honesty with customers, not advocacy against one's own client.

Correct. Revealing the seller's timing motivation breaches confidentiality, advising a lower offer breaches loyalty, and the counseling conduct may create an implied agency producing undisclosed dual agency.
A buyer representation agreement requires an agreement, not incidental advice.
Puffing concerns exaggerated opinion about the property, which is not what occurred.

questions.stem: Which event does NOT terminate an agency relationship?
options: Expiration of the listing term
Destruction of the property
The salesperson who took the listing leaving the brokerage
Mutual agreement of the parties
rationales: A listing ends on its stated termination date.
Destruction of the subject property makes performance impossible and ends the agency.
Correct. The listing belongs to the broker, so the departure of the individual salesperson does not terminate the agency between the broker and the client.
The parties may always agree to cancel.
